items.title: Debt-free with money in the bank, it’s time for BYU to strike
items.summary:
BYU coach Kalani Sitake, center, argues with a game official during game against Utah, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, in Salt Lake City. | Tyler Tate, Associated Press Imagine the bank calling with good news. First, they are dropping your two largest debts, and second, they are depositing interest money into your account from an earlier investment.

That’s pretty much what happened when the College Football Playoff rankings put BYU at No. 10 in this week’s poll.

Once the initial shock wore off, the facts became clear. The CFP committee was all but forgiving the Cougars of their two defeats — a 39-31 double-overtime stumble at UCF and last week’s 28-20 decision at Utah. At the same time, the group is rewarding BYU for last month’s 28-24 victory over No. 2 Notre Dame.

This makes the Cougars a happy customer. Even if they don’t qualify for the Big 12 championship game, which they still could, BYU still has a path to the playoffs by winning the last three games of the regular season — Baylor, at Kansas and Cincinnati.

Of course, BYU’s standing would be much better had they avoided road losses in Orlando and Salt Lake City. The reality is they weren’t good enough to win on those days; however, the idea that neither defeat was so bad that it cost them a shot at the playoffs means the Cougars can still get there. 

Nothing is guaranteed, but for BYU on Saturday, everything is required. They have been given a new lease on life — even born again. What appeared to be lost has been found — and returned.

But on Thursday night, the seniors’ accomplished careers came to a close.

No. 7 Clinton fell short in a 25-17, 25-15, 25-23 loss to No. 8 Monroe St. Mary’s Catholic Central in the Division 3 regional finals.

The Redwolves struggled to find a consistent rhythm offensively through the first two sets, which led to early deficits.

“When our passing is off, it’s a shock for everybody,” coach Kia Rainey said. “We’ve kind of been battling through that passing spurt for the past week now, and what a terrible week to have it.”

Clinton trailed 13-5 in the first set and 10-2 in the second. Despite showing improvement as the sets progressed, the Redwolves were unable to recover from their poor starts.

The third set was much more competitive. Clinton held a slim advantage early on before the Kestrels battled back to even the score at 11-11. SMCC began to pull away and took a 22-17 advantage, but the Redwolves showed resilience with a late rally. Clinton used a 4-1 run to cut the deficit to 23-21, prompting the Kestrels to call timeout.

“I would say overall, the whole energy and vibe was a lot different in the third set,” Rainey said. “I think they kind of finally settled in. A little too late, but they settled in.”

items.title: Former LSU championship winning coach returns to Tiger Stadium with Texas
items.summary:
Former LSU football defensive coordinator Will Muschamp will return to Baton Rouge on Saturday, this time leading Texas' defense. 

Muschamp was at LSU from 2001-04, playing a key role on Nick Saban's staff. With Muschamp calling the defense, LSU won the national title in 2003. 

In the years since, Muschamp has made several stops around the SEC, including head coaching stints at Florida and South Carolina. 

This won't be Muschamp's first return to LSU. He was Auburn's defensive coordinator in 2007 when Auburn came to Baton Rouge. As Florida's head coach, he led the Gators to Baton Rouge in 2011 and 2013. Muschamp came as Auburn's DC again in 2015 and as South Carolina's head coach in 2020. Muschamp is 0-5 in those games. 

Muschamp's Texas unit is one of the best in college football right now, only allowing 17.4 points per game.

items.title: Steeler who had Week 3 Burrow strip sack won't face Bengals | Report

Pittsburgh Steelers defensive tackle Derrick Harmon isn't expected to return from a foot injury to face the Cincinnati Bengals ahead of their NFL Week 10 showdown on NBC's Sunday Night Football at Paycor Stadium, according to the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette's Ray Fittipaldo .

Harmon hasn't played since suffering a foot injury Oct. 1 against Cleveland.

Harmon was considered the Steelers' biggest question mark for Week 10 on the team's injury report . He was designated to return from injured reserve and practiced Thursday and Friday, but was limited.

"We'll see by tomorrow," Harmon told reporters after Friday's practice.

With 53 seconds left in the Bengals' 30-27 loss to the Steelers in Pittsburgh in Week 3, Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow fumbled as he was sacked by Harmon at the Pittsburgh 46-yard line.

The ball was recovered by Pittsburgh's Sebastian Joseph-Day at the Cincinnati 49.

Harmon beat Bengals offensive lineman Dalton Risner to get to Burrow.

"We've got to be better," Burrow said after the game. "… You can't shoot yourself in the foot . Can't win in this league like that."

Bengals tight ends Erick All Jr. and Tanner Hudson were adamant after the game that All recovered Burrow's fumble. All said a Pittsburgh player was just laying on the ball, but it was All who secured it.

The call didn't go the Bengals' way.

You might have expected some partial concession to teammate Usman Khawaja’s depiction of endemic cheating, but Cummins was firm that this did not reflect the life he’d known. Once more with feeling, but more importantly with detail.

Media accounts will now depict this as Cummins and Khawaja at war, because a falling-out among friends is a juicy story to fatten up and serve for gluttony. It isn’t fair, because both have emphasised the importance of their friendship, strained as it must now be. As two thoughtful people with shared history, they have a better chance than most to find a way through.

items.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
items.summary:
Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award reveals a healthy revival

It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player. You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball.

These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Association launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wanderers’ then home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country and the FA secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, said he hoped it would finally break the barrier between those two worlds.

items.summary:
Left out of squad to tour South Africa, spin bowler’s exclusion points to a sport reshaped by the needs of T20 and hard data

During the summer, Sky Sports would frequently run an advert for one of English cricket’s blue-chip financial sponsors. I forget its exact name – something like WXYZ Tradify or Crypto Max 301 or Wealth Centaur would be my guess. But I remember there was a mind-shreddingly banal male voiceover (“diversify your forex contingents and start making your money bleed today”), to which England players like Harry Brook and Jacob Bethell were depicted engaging in various feats of staged cricketing heroism. Right up until the moment Shoaib Bashir steps up to bowl.

Bashir delivers his trademark off-break with that famously high release point. Upon which Bethell steps down the track and smashes the Wealth Centaur-branded ball back past his face, smashing a hole in the CGI wall and sending it into a hail of digital rain. Poor Shoaib. A passenger in the Ashes, sidelined for most of the home Test series, and now even getting clouted in the ad breaks. And in retrospect that was the point when we should all have realised that one English cricket’s weirder recent Test careers was already on borrowed time.
